title: Dogs around a sleeping lion
hookLine: the angry kings gather around Shishupala, Bhishma speaks of a sleeping lion, and Bhima has to be held back
carry: krodha: anger clouds the mind that sees
last: TRUE, KIND, HELPFUL SPEECH IS A TAPAS.

lines: TALK OF WAR AT THE RITE.
cards: A room can turn in a few seconds. One person's anger becomes a murmur, the murmur becomes a group, and the group starts talking about a fight. That's where the Rajasuya is now.

Other kings have gathered around Shishupala, and in the telling they begin to talk of war, of spoiling the rite before it's finished. Yudhishthira, the host, is worried, and he turns again to his grandfather.
Two kinds of anger in one hall: the kind that spreads, and the kind that has to be held back.

teach.b: It began with a dare. The youngest Pandava, Sahadeva, had challenged anyone who objected to the honor to answer him. Nobody did, but the grumbling only grew.
Now Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what to do about the kings. Bhishma isn't troubled.
He gives an image instead of a plan: these kings are like dogs barking around a sleeping lion, and the lion hasn't woken yet. Shishupala turns his anger on Bhishma.
He mocks the old man with a fable about a bird that preaches caution while picking scraps of meat from a lion's teeth, and he mocks the stories of Krishna's childhood too.
That's when Bhima rises, eyes blazing, ready to spring.
And Bhishma, the very man being insulted, holds him back and calms him down. Hinduism has a name for what Bhima is fighting.
Krodha, anger, is one of the six inner enemies Hindu teachers warn about, beside desire, greed, delusion, pride and envy.

teach.h: ANGER CLOUDS THE MIND THAT SEES.
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna traces the chain: wanting turns to anger, anger to confusion, confusion makes you forget what you know, and then judgment is lost. Look at the hall and you can watch it happen.
Shishupala's anger is past confusion; he can't see who's in front of him. Bhima's is climbing fast. Bhishma still remembers what the day is for, so he holds the anger instead of being held by it.
The teaching isn't that anger never comes. It's that it blinds, so it has to be caught before it acts. And Krishna, the sleeping lion in Bhishma's picture, still hasn't moved.

how: Krodha, anger, is counted among the six inner enemies (shadripu) in Hindu teaching, and the Bhagavad Gita (2.62–63) traces how desire turns to anger, and anger to confusion and lost judgment. Some retellings hold up Bhishma restraining Bhima, even while Shishupala mocks him, as a picture of an elder's self-control.

o: the brother whose rage Bhishma has to hold back
the king whose anger spreads, who mocks Bhishma
the youngest Pandava, who dares the hall to answer

games.q: in the angry hall — tap the pairs.
p: dogs barking around a sleeping lion
mocked Bhishma with a bird fable
rose in rage and was held back

s: in the Gita, anger leads to clearer judgment
Krishna says anger brings confusion, then forgetting, then the loss of judgment.
Bhishma held Bhima back, though Bhishma was the one insulted
the man being mocked is the one who calmed Bhima.
Bhishma compared the kings to sleeping lions
he compared them to dogs barking around a sleeping lion.

games.q: you're Bhishma. Shishupala has just mocked you before every king, and Bhima is rising to attack him. what do you do?
o: hold Bhima back and calm him.
games.why: the insulted elder holds Bhima back, catching krodha before it can turn the rite into a brawl.

practice: Bring to mind something that made you angry recently, and let yourself feel a little of it: the heat, the quickening.

Many Hindus meet that moment with a name of God, repeated quietly, Ram, Ram, or Om, so the mind has somewhere to stand. Try it now: one slow breath out, then the name, again and again, until the heat settles.
If you don't pray, use a slow count instead, and let each breath out run longer than the breath in.

wordCard.voice: Shishupala. The king whose anger spreads through the hall, who mocks Bhishma, and who stirs Bhima to a rage that Bhishma has to hold back.

orig.note: Sanskrit śiśupāla: the name of the king of Chedi, Krishna's cousin.

carryVoice: Your line: krodha: anger clouds the mind that sees. Bhishma caught it before it acted. Until tomorrow.
